# ZAWOOO — CTI Report

**Sample:** `33d3afddaa5710cdcc4e93a7bae8be010c19747fb53d85fcd54ef32056a1eb0b`
**Classification:** Ransomware, Linux/ELF64, NAS-specific (Synology DSM)
**Confidence:** High — conclusions drawn from static reverse engineering of the binary only, cross-verified in a second disassembler (Ghidra) for the footer layout, the XTS key schedule and every function boundary in the malware range.

## 1. Executive Summary

ZAWOOO is a dedicated Synology NAS encryptor, not a general-purpose Linux locker. Every design choice in it points at one target class: the directory exclusion list contains only Synology internal shares, the default scan root is the `/volume*` glob, and the fastest execution mode consumes a pre-built file index laid out under `/etc/f-index`.

The strategic point of interest for defenders is not the cryptography — which is correct and unbreakable without the operator's key — but the **two-stage encryption model**. A first "silent" run destroys file contents in place while leaving filenames intact and dropping no ransom note. The estate looks completely normal. Backups keep running and keep capturing already-encrypted data. A second run, whenever the operator chooses, recognises its own work from an 8-byte footer magic and does nothing but rename files and drop notes — turning an invisible compromise into a visible ransom event across a whole NAS in seconds.

This inverts the usual detection assumption. By the time ZAWOOO is visible, encryption is already old. The detection opportunity is entirely in the silent window, and it is a behavioural one: sustained strided read/write across large files, two new directories under `/etc`, and a lock file in `/var/run`.

Countering that, the payload itself is technically unremarkable: no packing, no obfuscation, no anti-debug, no anti-VM, no C2, no persistence, and a full debug logger with source filenames left compiled in. This is a well-thought-out playbook running on a mediocre codebase.

## 2. Actor Assessment

**What the code says about the operator**

| Observation | Assessment |
|---|---|
| A 16-hex victim ID compiled into the note template (redacted here) | One build per victim. The operator runs a builder and produces a bespoke binary per intrusion. Expect every sample to have a different RSA key, suffix and victim ID. |
| Per-build encryption suffix (`fHiQJervS`), with `SpXv2` / `MXvF0` visible as leftovers | Confirms at least three distinct builds of this family exist. Suffixes are random-looking 5–9 char tokens, so suffix-based detection will not generalise. |
| LockBit's Windows extension exclusion list embedded verbatim, typos included | The builder's configuration was copied from a LockBit-derived toolkit and never adapted. `.deskthemepack`, `.diagcab`, `.msstyes` are meaningless on DSM. Suggests an affiliate or a developer working from leaked/borrowed builder material rather than writing from scratch. |
| Two mutually inconsistent copies of the exclusion list left in the binary | Weak build hygiene; the codebase is edited by hand between builds and not regression-tested. |
| Compiled-in typos in filesystem paths (`/etc/slient-time`) | The path is part of the protocol between stages, so the typo is stable across builds and is a durable IOC. |
| `FTI_LOG` debug logger with `src/enc/thread.c` / `src/enc/work.c` and line numbers | The shipped payload is a debug build. Either the operator does not care, or they actively use the log to verify coverage during an engagement. |
| `-x` referenced in an error message but not implemented | Shared codebase across variants; feature flags come and go between builds. |
| GCC 11.2.1 20211120, static-pie, no DT_NEEDED | Deliberately built for appliance portability — it will run on any x86-64 DSM regardless of the libc version shipped by Synology. This is a considered choice, not an accident. |

**Note rhetoric.** The ransom note is a reputation-and-regulator play rather than a technical one. It leads with "a ransomware that prioritizes reputation", explicitly threatens notification of customers and of "the GDPR (Data Protection Authorities)", frames the ransom as cheaper than a breach fine, offers an intrusion debrief as a "security test", and coaches the victim at length on how to buy Bitcoin without alerting a broker. It also explicitly instructs the victim not to contact police or the FBI. This is European-facing extortion targeting organisations that hold customer data and are subject to GDPR — SMEs, MSPs, professional services, healthcare. The negotiation channel choice (Session + OnionMail, "send the message in two ways at the same time") indicates an operator expecting channel loss and running deliberately low-infrastructure.

**Capability ceiling.** The binary contains no networking code at all — no `connect`, no `sendto`, no C2. The note's exfiltration threat is therefore not backed by this sample. If data was stolen, it was stolen by separate tooling during the intrusion. Treat exfiltration claims as unverified-by-payload; verify independently from egress telemetry rather than assuming. Likewise there is no lateral movement, no credential access, no privilege escalation and no persistence in this binary. ZAWOOO is a terminal-stage payload dropped by hand onto an already-compromised appliance. Root (or at least write access to `/etc` and `/var/run`) is a prerequisite.

## 3. Attack Lifecycle

```
[ Initial access — not in this sample ]
        Internet-exposed DSM / QuickConnect / weak admin creds / n-day in DSM
                 |
                 v
[ Staging — partially inferred ]
        Operator builds /etc/f-index/<YYYY>/<MM>/index.dat inventory
        (records: u64 mtime | u64 size | u16 namelen | path)
        Writes /etc/f-index/baseline.stamp
                 |
                 v
[ Stage 1 — SILENT ]   ./enc -p /volume1 -s
        Creates /etc/slient-time/baseline.stamp (guarded clock, T)
        Encrypts file contents in place
        NO rename. NO ransom note. NO extension.
        -> NAS appears completely normal; backups capture ciphertext
                 |
                 v   ( operator-chosen delay )
[ Stage 2 — DETONATION ]   ./enc -p /volume1 -a      (or no flag)
        flock /var/run/enc-nas.lock
        Reads T from /etc/slient-time/baseline.stamp
        For each file with mtime >= T: footer magic present -> RENAME ONLY
        For everything else: full encrypt + rename
        Drops "How To Restore Your Files.txt" per directory
        -> whole estate visibly ransomed in the time of a rename() sweep
```

**Targeting priority.** `-a` mode does not scan the filesystem — it replays the index in an explicit newest-first order, logged by the binary itself:

```
phase 0 = _other (year>2026, newest)
phase 1 = month buckets 2026/12 .. 2000/01
phase 2 = _other (year<2000, oldest)
```

In parallel, a second producer `glob()`s `/volume*` and queues anything modified since the index was built. The consequence for defenders: the data the business touched most recently is destroyed first. A response that starts an hour into the encryption run has already lost the current working set. Speed of containment matters more here than for a locker that walks directories alphabetically.

## 4. Impact Assessment

| Dimension | Finding |
|---|---|
| Reversibility | None without the operator's RSA-2048 private key. Fresh 32-byte key per file from `/dev/urandom`, no key reuse, no PRNG weakness, no plaintext key retained on disk, key present only inside the RSA blob in each file's footer. |
| Filename recovery | Also impossible without the private key — the basename is XTS-encrypted with the same per-file key and the original is destroyed by `rename()`. Directory structure survives. |
| Data integrity | Partial by design. Only 6–25% of each file is ciphertext, but it is always the head and it is spread at a fixed stride, so container/archive/database formats are unusable. Do not assume "only 6% encrypted" means "94% recoverable". |
| Speed | Very high. 512 KB per 8 MB on files ≥ 64 MB, three worker threads, index-driven ordering. A multi-terabyte NAS is destroyed in a fraction of the time a full-encryption locker would need. |
| Availability of DSM | Preserved deliberately. Synology system directories are excluded so the appliance stays bootable and the web UI reachable — the operator wants the victim able to read the note and negotiate. |
| Backups | Primary risk. Any backup taken during the silent stage contains ciphertext with valid-looking filenames. Backup jobs will report success. Snapshot retention windows may be entirely poisoned before anyone knows an incident occurred. |
| Recovery paths that survive | Synology/Btrfs snapshots and off-box replicas are not touched — the binary contains no snapshot, backup or log tampering whatsoever. Immutable/off-appliance copies predating the silent stage are the realistic recovery route. |

## 5. Detection Engineering

**File-based — encrypted artefacts.** Every encrypted file ends with a 12-byte tail: a u32 footer length followed by the 8-byte magic. This is exact, cheap, and independent of the per-build suffix.

```yara
rule ZAWOOO_Encrypted_File
{
    meta:
        description = "File encrypted by ZAWOOO - footer magic"
    condition:
        filesize > 268 and
        uint32be(filesize - 8) == 0xDFB307AC and
        uint32be(filesize - 4) == 0x09272154
}
```

Because silent mode does not rename, this rule is the only file-level way to detect stage-1 compromise. Run it across NAS shares and, critically, across backup sets. It does not cover the earlier file format. Dead-but-present code in this sample (`0x83E0`, `0xB740`) shows a prior build that appended a bare 256-byte RSA blob with no magic and no length field, and that kept the original filename with the suffix appended (`report.xlsx.<suffix>`). To hunt those, look for double extensions where the second component matches a short random-looking token, and for files whose last 256 bytes are high-entropy while the rest of the file is not. Since the builder still ships this code path, a future build could re-enable it — do not treat the magic as a permanent family invariant.

**File-based — the payload.**

```yara
rule ZAWOOO_Linux_NAS_Encryptor
{
    meta:
        description = "ZAWOOO Synology NAS ransomware (ELF64 static-pie)"
    strings:
        $magic   = { DF B3 07 AC 09 27 21 54 B1 E1 3B 58 7F 52 13 DE }
        $lock    = "/var/run/enc-nas.lock"              ascii
        $slient  = "/etc/slient-time/baseline.stamp"    ascii
        $findex  = "/etc/f-index/baseline.stamp"        ascii
        $note    = "How To Restore Your Files.txt"      ascii
        $log1    = "src/enc/thread.c"                   ascii
        $log2    = "src/enc/work.c"                     ascii
        $usage   = "usage: %s -p path"                  ascii
        $typo1   = "alredy run(-x ), exit"              ascii
        $typo2   = "xts encrypt fail: -0x%04X"          ascii
        $syno    = "@SynoFinder-etc-volume"             ascii
    condition:
        uint32(0) == 0x464C457F and filesize < 4MB and 3 of them
}
```

The `src/enc/*.c` strings and the `slient` typo are the most build-durable anchors: they are compiled-in paths and log format strings, not configuration, so they should survive across builds that change the RSA key, suffix and victim ID.

**Host telemetry**

| Signal | Rationale |
|---|---|
| `/etc/slient-time/` created (mode 0755) | Not a Synology path. Its existence alone means stage 1 ran or is running. Highest-value single indicator. |
| `/etc/f-index/` created, containing `<YYYY>/<MM>/index.dat` | Pre-encryption staging. Detecting this catches the intrusion before any file is touched. |
| `/var/run/enc-nas.lock` present, or an exclusive flock held on it | Stage 2 in progress. |
| `How To Restore Your Files.txt` written to many directories | Stage 2 complete. Late signal. |
| Mass `rename()` matching `^[0-9A-F]{16}\.[A-Za-z0-9_]{3,12}$` | Stage 2 in progress. |
| One process, sustained `open(O_RDWR)` then lseek/read/write pairs at a fixed stride (4 MB or 8 MB) over many large files | Stage 1 in progress — the only high-fidelity behavioural signal during the silent window. |
| `sh -c "date +%s"` spawned by a non-shell long-running binary | Clock source of last resort; unusual on an appliance. |
| Repeated `open("/dev/urandom")` at file-processing cadence | One open per encrypted file; a distinctive rate signature. |

**Network telemetry.** None from the payload. Do not build detections expecting ZAWOOO C2 — there is none. Focus network hunting on the intrusion that delivered it (DSM admin authentication from unusual sources, QuickConnect/relay usage, SSH enablement) and on egress that would indicate the separate exfiltration tooling the note implies.

## 6. Hunting Guidance

Run these on Synology appliances and any Linux host with NAS shares.

```bash
# 1. Stage-1 marker directories — the two highest-value checks
ls -la /etc/slient-time/ /etc/f-index/ 2>/dev/null
cat /etc/slient-time/baseline.stamp 2>/dev/null   # epoch: when silent mode started

# 2. Stage-2 lock
ls -la /var/run/enc-nas.lock 2>/dev/null
fuser -v /var/run/enc-nas.lock 2>/dev/null

# 3. Silently encrypted files — footer magic, name unchanged
find /volume1 -type f -size +268c -print0 2>/dev/null \
  | xargs -0 -P4 -I{} sh -c \
    'tail -c 8 "$1" | od -An -tx1 | tr -d " \n" | grep -q "^dfb307ac09272154$" && echo "ENCRYPTED: $1"' _ {}

# 4. Renamed files (stage 2)
find /volume* -type f -regextype posix-extended \
     -regex '.*/[0-9A-F]{16}\.[A-Za-z0-9_]{3,12}$' 2>/dev/null | head

# 5. Ransom notes
find /volume* -name 'How To Restore Your Files.txt' 2>/dev/null | head

# 6. Any process holding many large files open read-write
ls -l /proc/*/fd 2>/dev/null | grep -E '/volume[0-9]' | head -50
```

If step 3 returns hits while steps 4 and 5 return nothing, you are inside the silent window. That is the single most valuable outcome of this hunt: contain immediately, and treat every backup taken since `/etc/slient-time/baseline.stamp` as suspect.

## 7. Response Guidance

1. Isolate the appliance at the network layer before anything else. Do not shut it down cleanly if stage 2 is running — a graceful stop lets in-flight writes complete. Pull the network first, then decide.
2. Read `/etc/slient-time/baseline.stamp`. It is a plain epoch. It tells you when silent encryption began, which directly scopes the backup poisoning window.
3. Do not restore from any backup taken after that timestamp without first validating it with the `ZAWOOO_Encrypted_File` rule. Backups from the silent window contain ciphertext under correct filenames and will restore cleanly and uselessly.
4. Check `/etc/f-index/`. Its `index.dat` files are a complete inventory of what the operator enumerated — effectively a free scoping document for the incident, including the size and mtime of every file they intended to encrypt.
5. Preserve, do not delete, encrypted files. Each footer holds the RSA-wrapped per-file key; if the private key is ever recovered by law enforcement, those files are decryptable. Deleting them forecloses that option permanently.
6. Check Btrfs/Synology snapshots and off-box replicas. The binary does not touch them. If snapshots predate the silent stage, they are the realistic recovery route.
7. Collect the binary and any stderr capture. If the operator ran it with `FTI_LOG` set, the log is a per-file record of exactly what was encrypted.
8. Do not assume no exfiltration, and do not assume exfiltration. The payload has no network capability; any data theft used separate tooling. Determine this from egress telemetry, not from the note.

## 8. Assessment Notes & Gaps

| Item | Status |
|---|---|
| Who builds `/etc/f-index` | Unknown. Not created by this binary. Either a separate staging tool or repurposed Synology indexer output. Recovering that tool would materially improve early detection. |
| The `_F` and `c2w`/`ctw` suffix variants | Unresolved. The note promises three suffixes; this build emits one. Self-exclusion entries from sibling builds follow a `<base>` / `<base>_F` / `c2w|ctw` pattern, implying companion binaries not present in this sample set. |
| Earlier file format (v1) | Recovered from dead code. `zw_write_footer_v1_dead @ 0x83E0` and `zw_rename_append_suffix_v1_dead @ 0xB740` are compiled in but unreferenced. They describe an earlier build that appended a bare 256-byte RSA blob (no magic, no length) and appended the suffix to the original filename instead of replacing it. Files from that build are invisible to the footer-magic rule. |
| Exfiltration capability | Absent from this binary. Claims in the note are unverified by code. |
| Initial access vector | Out of scope for a payload-only analysis. |
| Group attribution | Not attempted. Conclusions here derive from the binary alone; the LockBit exclusion list indicates borrowed builder configuration, not a LockBit affiliation. |
| Build date | Inferred only. The hardcoded clock fallback `1784990000 = 2026-07-25T14:33:20Z` sits inside the accepted execution window and is the closest available proxy. |

**Tracking recommendations.** Pivot on the RSA SPKI hash `66e37055247446e1f23efe62cf011b8cf77aa8aa0a937469319a5d8ce9053004` to link samples that share a key. A shared key across victims would indicate a single operator rather than an affiliate programme. Pivot on the 16-byte tweak constant `DF B3 07 AC 09 27 21 54 B1 E1 3B 58 7F 52 13 DE`. If it is stable across builds it is the best cross-build anchor available; if it varies, it becomes a per-build fingerprint. Watch the DLS onion for victim postings to correlate with the hardcoded victim ID model.

# LockBit 5.0 (x64 hardened — "Corteva/Solstice" lure) — Technical Analysis Report

## 1. Key Judgements

This analysis identifies a **LockBit 5.0-generation x64 hardened build** featuring full obfuscation protections distinct from older 3.0-base variants. The sample masquerades as "Corteva / Solstice Google Photos" with administrator elevation request—a social-engineering distribution tactic.

The decrypted payload reveals a modern cryptographic stack: **X25519 key wrapping combined with ChaCha20-20 file encryption and Keccak-f1600/SHAKE256 key derivation**. This represents a significant departure from Sample 1's older SSSE3-ChaCha(22)+RSA-1024 approach.

The payload demonstrates extensive operational capabilities including multi-threaded chunked file encryption, RunPE process-hollowing targeting defrag.exe/svchost, ETW bypass, network self-propagation through ARP enumeration and port-scanning, event-log clearing, and service/process termination. A critical operator-origin signal emerges: the malware aborts execution on Russian-locale systems (UILang `0x419`) and specific GeoID values, consistent with CIS-exclusion patterns typical of LockBit RaaS affiliates.

Embedded configuration was successfully decrypted, revealing target drive scope, exclusion lists, VM-disk targeting (vhdx/avhdx), complete CLI argument sets, and operation-mode keywords. The ransom note and three onion addresses are MBA-encoded and assembled at runtime rather than embedded statically.

## 2. Actor / Tooling Assessment

The operator deploys the **modern LockBit 5.0 toolchain** with per-build customization:

- **Tailored masquerade:** Each build receives campaign-specific lure metadata while reusing the protected 5.0 core
- **Anti-analysis defenses:** The combination of MBA obfuscation, global-PRNG opaque predicates, import-by-hash, and per-string runtime crypto renders automated unpackers and sandbox analysis nearly ineffective
- **Elevation expectations:** The `requireAdministrator` manifest indicates the operator expects either user-initiated launch or exploitation of a delivery chain with elevation privileges

Existing LockBit 3.0 detection content—built around config-blob YARA signatures and residual templates—will not trigger on this 5.0-generation build.

## 3. Capability Summary

| Capability | Status |
|---|---|
| Masquerade / fake product identity | Confirmed — Corteva / Solstice Google Photos (resources) |
| Admin elevation request | Confirmed — manifest `requireAdministrator` |
| MBA obfuscation | Confirmed |
| Global-PRNG opaque predicates | Confirmed |
| Per-string runtime decryption + cache | Confirmed — 28 IDs / 78 sites |
| Import-by-hash (empty IAT) | Confirmed |
| Encrypted on-file string/config pool | Confirmed — .rdata ≈ 541 KB, entropy ≈ 8.00 |
| Monolithic packer (loader) | Absent |
| **File-encryption cipher** | **Confirmed — ChaCha20 (standard, 20-round, 256-bit)** |
| **Key wrap** | **Confirmed — X25519 (Curve25519 ECDH)** |
| **KDF / integrity** | **Confirmed — SHAKE256 / Keccak-f1600** |
| Chunked / partial encryption | Confirmed — `EncryptPartly`, chunk map + FILEMETA footer |
| RunPE process-hollowing | Confirmed — target string `\defrag.\svchost`; defrag.exe execution observed live |
| ETW bypass | Confirmed — `"Etw not patched!"` at payload startup |
| Network self-propagation (code present) | Confirmed in code — ARP + subnet enum + async port-scan; mapped drive encryption observed live |
| Event-log clearing | Confirmed — EvtOpenSession channel enumeration |
| Service / process kill | Confirmed — SCM enum + process-kill failed-cache |
| Geo / UI-language fence | Confirmed — abort on UILang `0x419` (Russian) / GeoID `0xC9` |
| Operation-mode flag | Confirmed — default `0x0A`; modes: local/net/all |
| CLI / target arguments | Confirmed — semicolon-delimited wide path list |
| Recovery inhibition (VSS shadow delete) | Confirmed — dynamic vssapi.dll+ole32.dll, COM IVssBackupComponents |
| Persistence / mutex / self-delete | Not found |
| Embedded config | Recovered — XOR `0x57++` keystream cracked |
| VM-disk targeting | Confirmed — vhdx / avhdx in target list |
| Onions / note body | Recovered from detonation (runtime-MBA-assembled) |

## 4. Behavioural Profile

The decrypted payload exposes behaviour statically through debug strings:

**Impact:** Multi-threaded chunked file encryption using ChaCha20 body cipher with per-file X25519-wrapped keys, per-chunk SHAKE256-derived keystreams, and Keccak integrity hashes. FILEMETA footer appended. Ransom note `ReadMeForDecrypt.txt` dropped. → T1486.

**Defense evasion:** RunPE process-hollowing into defrag.exe/svchost (T1055.012); ETW patching at startup (T1562.006); Windows event-log clearing (T1070.001).

**Inhibit recovery:** VSS shadow-copy deletion via dynamically-loaded vssapi.dll + ole32.dll (COM IVssBackupComponents, avoiding command-line telemetry) (T1490); service stop + process termination with failed-kill cache (T1489).

**Propagation (SMB lateral movement—code-evidenced):** Network spreader contains host discovery via GetIpNetTable (ARP) + subnet enumeration feeding async ConnectEx/IOCP port-scanning for file encryption on ADMIN$/SMB shares (T1021.002 / T1135). Live observation confirmed mapped network drives N:/M: mounted and encrypted. Active socket scanning not observed in isolated lab. Geo + UI-language fence executes before operational code.

## 5. Detection & Hunting Guidance

**On-disk / static:**
- Hash-block SHA-256 / MD5
- **Masquerade hunt:** Files presenting as "Solstice Google Photos.exe" with CompanyName "Corteva" and ProductName "Solstice Google Photos" lacking legitimate vendor signatures; flag combination with `requireAdministrator` manifest and empty import table
- **Structural hunt:** PE32+ with empty IAT, single high-entropy .rdata (~0.5 MB, entropy ≈ 8.0), and .data virtual size in multi-MB range over ~1 KB raw size

**Behavioural / runtime (EDR):**
- Process performing RunPE process-hollowing into defrag.exe/svchost with plaintext target string `\defrag.\svchost`
- ETW provider tampering followed by Windows event-log clearing (EvtOpenSession / EvtClearLog)
- Shadow-copy deletion via COM (vssapi.dll + ole32.dll loading by non-backup process)
- Mass file modification with FILEMETA footer + `ReadMeForDecrypt.txt` ransom note
- Internal port-scanning / ARP enumeration / SMB share access from single process
- Service-control enumeration + bulk process termination preceding encryption
- Process memory capture for runtime-only IOCs (onions, note text, public key)

**Network:** Pivot on internal port-scan / ARP spread behaviour rather than static C2.

## 6. Operational Comparison with 3.0-base lineage

| Concern | S1 (3.0-base) | S3 (5.0, this report) |
|---|---|---|
| Harvest config from file | Yes | Yes — operational config decrypted; onion/note/key not embedded |
| 3.0 detection content effective | Yes | **No** |
| Static unpack yields payload | Yes (APLib blob) | **No loader unpack (per-string); payload recovered by emulation** |
| Distinctive host IOC at rest | onions/note | **masquerade identity + structural** |
| Time-to-IOC | Low | **Moderate (lure metadata + decrypted config help)** |

## 7. Analytical Confidence & Gaps

**High confidence:** LockBit 5.0-generation x64 identity; obfuscation architecture; loader decryptor (28-ID inventory); absence of monolithic packer; masquerade identity; payload crypto stack (X25519 + ChaCha20-20 + Keccak/SHAKE256) + key-derivation chain; payload file-encryption pipeline; payload behaviour map; decrypted operational config.

**Acknowledged gap:** Runtime configuration elements—onion endpoints, ransom-note body, victim/campaign public key, target-extension/exclusion lists, command-line interface, and behaviour-flag map—are inlined into the 83 KB MBA entry monolith and materialize at runtime only. The **file-cipher identity gap is now CLOSED** (prior report's main open item). Closing remaining gaps requires API-faithful emulator extension or contained-detonation memory capture.

## 8. Recommendations

1. **Block** file hashes; deploy masquerade hunt (Corteva/Solstice version-info + `requireAdministrator` + empty IAT) and structural family hunt
2. **Alert** users to "Solstice Google Photos update" lure theme; treat unexpected admin-elevation prompts as malicious
3. **Update IR playbooks** for LB 5.0: assume no static config; add contained detonation + process-memory forensics
4. **Re-validate** LockBit 3.0-focused detection content—ineffective on this variant

## 9. Indicators of Compromise

**File Hashes:**
- SHA-256: `6d0166d181db1f6c381c3ff5fff4fe4106fbc17bc29316e3cf3f65136ee4803c`

**Structural Indicators:**

**Behavioural Indicators:**

**Cryptography:**

**Embedded Configuration:**

# Rhysida — CTI Report (OSINT)

## Resumen ejecutivo
Rhysida es un grupo de ransomware con modelo RaaS y doble extorsion, activo desde mayo de 2023. Es conocido por ataques de alto impacto a sanidad, educacion y sector publico. Sus TTPs solapan de forma marcada con Vice Society, lo que apunta a una evolucion o rebrand de ese ecosistema.

## Aparicion y modelo
- Primeras publicaciones: mayo 2023. RaaS con programa de afiliados.
- Doble extorsion: robo de datos previo al cifrado y subasta/publicacion en su DLS (.onion).
- Objeto de una alerta conjunta CISA/FBI (#StopRansomware, AA23-319A).

## Atribucion / origen
- Fuerte solapamiento de TTPs e infraestructura con Vice Society (probable continuidad).
- Operadores de habla rusa (atribucion de baja-media confianza).

## Objetivos (sectores y regiones)
- Sanidad, educacion, gobierno y manufactura. Actividad global con foco en EEUU y Europa.

## Victimas notables
- British Library (Reino Unido, 2023, confirmado por la propia biblioteca).
- Prospect Medical Holdings (hospitales, EEUU, 2023).
- Insomniac Games (Sony), Ejercito de Chile, City of Columbus (Ohio).

- **Acceso inicial:** phishing, cuentas validas y VPN; explotacion de servicios expuestos.
- **Movimiento lateral:** Cobalt Strike, PsExec y RDP.
- **Evasion / anti-recuperacion:** script tipo "SILENTKILL", borrado de shadow copies, desactivacion de AV.
- **Cifrado:** ChaCha20 con clave RSA; extension `.rhysida`; nota `CriticalBreachDetected.pdf`.
- **Exfiltracion:** herramientas de sincronizacion antes del cifrado.

## Deteccion y recomendaciones
- Vigilar Cobalt Strike, uso anomalo de PsExec/RDP y `vssadmin delete shadows`.
- MFA en VPN/RDP; parcheo de servicios expuestos; copias inmutables/offline.

Pear es un grupo de **extorsion por robo de datos** (sin cifrado) aparecido a mediados de 2025. Opera como equipo cerrado, con foco en organizaciones estadounidenses de sectores legal, sanitario, financiero y educativo.

- Mediados de 2025; debut con ~20 victimas publicadas a la vez en su DLS en Tor.
- Modelo de solo extorsion: roba datos y extorsiona sin desplegar cifrado ni malware. Equipo privado, sin afiliados.

- Se presenta como equipo independiente sin relacion con otros actores; sin solapamiento tecnico identificado.

- Legal (hasta ~20% de incidentes), sanidad, servicios financieros y educacion superior.
- ~90% de victimas en EEUU; resto en Alemania, Egipto, Suiza, Australia y Nueva Zelanda. Organizaciones de 2 a 5.000+ empleados, en su mayoria por debajo de 5M USD de ingresos.

- Tri-Century Eye Care (~200.000 personas), Iroquois Memorial Hospital (~3,5 TB), Monmouth University (~6 TB), proveedor de software de automocion (750.000+ personas).

library.report_md:
# ZAWOOO — CTI Report

**Sample:** `33d3afddaa5710cdcc4e93a7bae8be010c19747fb53d85fcd54ef32056a1eb0b`
**Classification:** Ransomware, Linux/ELF64, NAS-specific (Synology DSM)
**Confidence:** High — conclusions drawn from static reverse engineering of the binary only, cross-verified in a second disassembler (Ghidra) for the footer layout, the XTS key schedule and every function boundary in the malware range.

## 1. Executive Summary

ZAWOOO is a dedicated Synology NAS encryptor, not a general-purpose Linux locker. Every design choice in it points at one target class: the directory exclusion list contains only Synology internal shares, the default scan root is the `/volume*` glob, and the fastest execution mode consumes a pre-built file index laid out under `/etc/f-index`.

The strategic point of interest for defenders is not the cryptography — which is correct and unbreakable without the operator's key — but the **two-stage encryption model**. A first "silent" run destroys file contents in place while leaving filenames intact and dropping no ransom note. The estate looks completely normal. Backups keep running and keep capturing already-encrypted data. A second run, whenever the operator chooses, recognises its own work from an 8-byte footer magic and does nothing but rename files and drop notes — turning an invisible compromise into a visible ransom event across a whole NAS in seconds.

This inverts the usual detection assumption. By the time ZAWOOO is visible, encryption is already old. The detection opportunity is entirely in the silent window, and it is a behavioural one: sustained strided read/write across large files, two new directories under `/etc`, and a lock file in `/var/run`.

Countering that, the payload itself is technically unremarkable: no packing, no obfuscation, no anti-debug, no anti-VM, no C2, no persistence, and a full debug logger with source filenames left compiled in. This is a well-thought-out playbook running on a mediocre codebase.

## 2. Actor Assessment

**What the code says about the operator**

| Observation | Assessment |
|---|---|
| A 16-hex victim ID compiled into the note template (redacted here) | One build per victim. The operator runs a builder and produces a bespoke binary per intrusion. Expect every sample to have a different RSA key, suffix and victim ID. |
| Per-build encryption suffix (`fHiQJervS`), with `SpXv2` / `MXvF0` visible as leftovers | Confirms at least three distinct builds of this family exist. Suffixes are random-looking 5–9 char tokens, so suffix-based detection will not generalise. |
| LockBit's Windows extension exclusion list embedded verbatim, typos included | The builder's configuration was copied from a LockBit-derived toolkit and never adapted. `.deskthemepack`, `.diagcab`, `.msstyes` are meaningless on DSM. Suggests an affiliate or a developer working from leaked/borrowed builder material rather than writing from scratch. |
| Two mutually inconsistent copies of the exclusion list left in the binary | Weak build hygiene; the codebase is edited by hand between builds and not regression-tested. |
| Compiled-in typos in filesystem paths (`/etc/slient-time`) | The path is part of the protocol between stages, so the typo is stable across builds and is a durable IOC. |
| `FTI_LOG` debug logger with `src/enc/thread.c` / `src/enc/work.c` and line numbers | The shipped payload is a debug build. Either the operator does not care, or they actively use the log to verify coverage during an engagement. |
| `-x` referenced in an error message but not implemented | Shared codebase across variants; feature flags come and go between builds. |
| GCC 11.2.1 20211120, static-pie, no DT_NEEDED | Deliberately built for appliance portability — it will run on any x86-64 DSM regardless of the libc version shipped by Synology. This is a considered choice, not an accident. |

**Note rhetoric.** The ransom note is a reputation-and-regulator play rather than a technical one. It leads with "a ransomware that prioritizes reputation", explicitly threatens notification of customers and of "the GDPR (Data Protection Authorities)", frames the ransom as cheaper than a breach fine, offers an intrusion debrief as a "security test", and coaches the victim at length on how to buy Bitcoin without alerting a broker. It also explicitly instructs the victim not to contact police or the FBI. This is European-facing extortion targeting organisations that hold customer data and are subject to GDPR — SMEs, MSPs, professional services, healthcare. The negotiation channel choice (Session + OnionMail, "send the message in two ways at the same time") indicates an operator expecting channel loss and running deliberately low-infrastructure.

**Capability ceiling.** The binary contains no networking code at all — no `connect`, no `sendto`, no C2. The note's exfiltration threat is therefore not backed by this sample. If data was stolen, it was stolen by separate tooling during the intrusion. Treat exfiltration claims as unverified-by-payload; verify independently from egress telemetry rather than assuming. Likewise there is no lateral movement, no credential access, no privilege escalation and no persistence in this binary. ZAWOOO is a terminal-stage payload dropped by hand onto an already-compromised appliance. Root (or at least write access to `/etc` and `/var/run`) is a prerequisite.

## 3. Attack Lifecycle

```
[ Initial access — not in this sample ]
        Internet-exposed DSM / QuickConnect / weak admin creds / n-day in DSM
                 |
                 v
[ Staging — partially inferred ]
        Operator builds /etc/f-index/<YYYY>/<MM>/index.dat inventory
        (records: u64 mtime | u64 size | u16 namelen | path)
        Writes /etc/f-index/baseline.stamp
                 |
                 v
[ Stage 1 — SILENT ]   ./enc -p /volume1 -s
        Creates /etc/slient-time/baseline.stamp (guarded clock, T)
        Encrypts file contents in place
        NO rename. NO ransom note. NO extension.
        -> NAS appears completely normal; backups capture ciphertext
                 |
                 v   ( operator-chosen delay )
[ Stage 2 — DETONATION ]   ./enc -p /volume1 -a      (or no flag)
        flock /var/run/enc-nas.lock
        Reads T from /etc/slient-time/baseline.stamp
        For each file with mtime >= T: footer magic present -> RENAME ONLY
        For everything else: full encrypt + rename
        Drops "How To Restore Your Files.txt" per directory
        -> whole estate visibly ransomed in the time of a rename() sweep
```

**Targeting priority.** `-a` mode does not scan the filesystem — it replays the index in an explicit newest-first order, logged by the binary itself:

```
phase 0 = _other (year>2026, newest)
phase 1 = month buckets 2026/12 .. 2000/01
phase 2 = _other (year<2000, oldest)
```

In parallel, a second producer `glob()`s `/volume*` and queues anything modified since the index was built. The consequence for defenders: the data the business touched most recently is destroyed first. A response that starts an hour into the encryption run has already lost the current working set. Speed of containment matters more here than for a locker that walks directories alphabetically.

## 4. Impact Assessment

| Dimension | Finding |
|---|---|
| Reversibility | None without the operator's RSA-2048 private key. Fresh 32-byte key per file from `/dev/urandom`, no key reuse, no PRNG weakness, no plaintext key retained on disk, key present only inside the RSA blob in each file's footer. |
| Filename recovery | Also impossible without the private key — the basename is XTS-encrypted with the same per-file key and the original is destroyed by `rename()`. Directory structure survives. |
| Data integrity | Partial by design. Only 6–25% of each file is ciphertext, but it is always the head and it is spread at a fixed stride, so container/archive/database formats are unusable. Do not assume "only 6% encrypted" means "94% recoverable". |
| Speed | Very high. 512 KB per 8 MB on files ≥ 64 MB, three worker threads, index-driven ordering. A multi-terabyte NAS is destroyed in a fraction of the time a full-encryption locker would need. |
| Availability of DSM | Preserved deliberately. Synology system directories are excluded so the appliance stays bootable and the web UI reachable — the operator wants the victim able to read the note and negotiate. |
| Backups | Primary risk. Any backup taken during the silent stage contains ciphertext with valid-looking filenames. Backup jobs will report success. Snapshot retention windows may be entirely poisoned before anyone knows an incident occurred. |
| Recovery paths that survive | Synology/Btrfs snapshots and off-box replicas are not touched — the binary contains no snapshot, backup or log tampering whatsoever. Immutable/off-appliance copies predating the silent stage are the realistic recovery route. |

## 5. Detection Engineering

**File-based — encrypted artefacts.** Every encrypted file ends with a 12-byte tail: a u32 footer length followed by the 8-byte magic. This is exact, cheap, and independent of the per-build suffix.

```yara
rule ZAWOOO_Encrypted_File
{
    meta:
        description = "File encrypted by ZAWOOO - footer magic"
    condition:
        filesize > 268 and
        uint32be(filesize - 8) == 0xDFB307AC and
        uint32be(filesize - 4) == 0x09272154
}
```

Because silent mode does not rename, this rule is the only file-level way to detect stage-1 compromise. Run it across NAS shares and, critically, across backup sets. It does not cover the earlier file format. Dead-but-present code in this sample (`0x83E0`, `0xB740`) shows a prior build that appended a bare 256-byte RSA blob with no magic and no length field, and that kept the original filename with the suffix appended (`report.xlsx.<suffix>`). To hunt those, look for double extensions where the second component matches a short random-looking token, and for files whose last 256 bytes are high-entropy while the rest of the file is not. Since the builder still ships this code path, a future build could re-enable it — do not treat the magic as a permanent family invariant.

**File-based — the payload.**

```yara
rule ZAWOOO_Linux_NAS_Encryptor
{
    meta:
        description = "ZAWOOO Synology NAS ransomware (ELF64 static-pie)"
    strings:
        $magic   = { DF B3 07 AC 09 27 21 54 B1 E1 3B 58 7F 52 13 DE }
        $lock    = "/var/run/enc-nas.lock"              ascii
        $slient  = "/etc/slient-time/baseline.stamp"    ascii
        $findex  = "/etc/f-index/baseline.stamp"        ascii
        $note    = "How To Restore Your Files.txt"      ascii
        $log1    = "src/enc/thread.c"                   ascii
        $log2    = "src/enc/work.c"                     ascii
        $usage   = "usage: %s -p path"                  ascii
        $typo1   = "alredy run(-x ), exit"              ascii
        $typo2   = "xts encrypt fail: -0x%04X"          ascii
        $syno    = "@SynoFinder-etc-volume"             ascii
    condition:
        uint32(0) == 0x464C457F and filesize < 4MB and 3 of them
}
```

The `src/enc/*.c` strings and the `slient` typo are the most build-durable anchors: they are compiled-in paths and log format strings, not configuration, so they should survive across builds that change the RSA key, suffix and victim ID.

**Host telemetry**

| Signal | Rationale |
|---|---|
| `/etc/slient-time/` created (mode 0755) | Not a Synology path. Its existence alone means stage 1 ran or is running. Highest-value single indicator. |
| `/etc/f-index/` created, containing `<YYYY>/<MM>/index.dat` | Pre-encryption staging. Detecting this catches the intrusion before any file is touched. |
| `/var/run/enc-nas.lock` present, or an exclusive flock held on it | Stage 2 in progress. |
| `How To Restore Your Files.txt` written to many directories | Stage 2 complete. Late signal. |
| Mass `rename()` matching `^[0-9A-F]{16}\.[A-Za-z0-9_]{3,12}$` | Stage 2 in progress. |
| One process, sustained `open(O_RDWR)` then lseek/read/write pairs at a fixed stride (4 MB or 8 MB) over many large files | Stage 1 in progress — the only high-fidelity behavioural signal during the silent window. |
| `sh -c "date +%s"` spawned by a non-shell long-running binary | Clock source of last resort; unusual on an appliance. |
| Repeated `open("/dev/urandom")` at file-processing cadence | One open per encrypted file; a distinctive rate signature. |

**Network telemetry.** None from the payload. Do not build detections expecting ZAWOOO C2 — there is none. Focus network hunting on the intrusion that delivered it (DSM admin authentication from unusual sources, QuickConnect/relay usage, SSH enablement) and on egress that would indicate the separate exfiltration tooling the note implies.

## 6. Hunting Guidance

Run these on Synology appliances and any Linux host with NAS shares.

```bash
# 1. Stage-1 marker directories — the two highest-value checks
ls -la /etc/slient-time/ /etc/f-index/ 2>/dev/null
cat /etc/slient-time/baseline.stamp 2>/dev/null   # epoch: when silent mode started

# 2. Stage-2 lock
ls -la /var/run/enc-nas.lock 2>/dev/null
fuser -v /var/run/enc-nas.lock 2>/dev/null

# 3. Silently encrypted files — footer magic, name unchanged
find /volume1 -type f -size +268c -print0 2>/dev/null \
  | xargs -0 -P4 -I{} sh -c \
    'tail -c 8 "$1" | od -An -tx1 | tr -d " \n" | grep -q "^dfb307ac09272154$" && echo "ENCRYPTED: $1"' _ {}

# 4. Renamed files (stage 2)
find /volume* -type f -regextype posix-extended \
     -regex '.*/[0-9A-F]{16}\.[A-Za-z0-9_]{3,12}$' 2>/dev/null | head

# 5. Ransom notes
find /volume* -name 'How To Restore Your Files.txt' 2>/dev/null | head

# 6. Any process holding many large files open read-write
ls -l /proc/*/fd 2>/dev/null | grep -E '/volume[0-9]' | head -50
```

If step 3 returns hits while steps 4 and 5 return nothing, you are inside the silent window. That is the single most valuable outcome of this hunt: contain immediately, and treat every backup taken since `/etc/slient-time/baseline.stamp` as suspect.

## 7. Response Guidance

1. Isolate the appliance at the network layer before anything else. Do not shut it down cleanly if stage 2 is running — a graceful stop lets in-flight writes complete. Pull the network first, then decide.
2. Read `/etc/slient-time/baseline.stamp`. It is a plain epoch. It tells you when silent encryption began, which directly scopes the backup poisoning window.
3. Do not restore from any backup taken after that timestamp without first validating it with the `ZAWOOO_Encrypted_File` rule. Backups from the silent window contain ciphertext under correct filenames and will restore cleanly and uselessly.
4. Check `/etc/f-index/`. Its `index.dat` files are a complete inventory of what the operator enumerated — effectively a free scoping document for the incident, including the size and mtime of every file they intended to encrypt.
5. Preserve, do not delete, encrypted files. Each footer holds the RSA-wrapped per-file key; if the private key is ever recovered by law enforcement, those files are decryptable. Deleting them forecloses that option permanently.
6. Check Btrfs/Synology snapshots and off-box replicas. The binary does not touch them. If snapshots predate the silent stage, they are the realistic recovery route.
7. Collect the binary and any stderr capture. If the operator ran it with `FTI_LOG` set, the log is a per-file record of exactly what was encrypted.
8. Do not assume no exfiltration, and do not assume exfiltration. The payload has no network capability; any data theft used separate tooling. Determine this from egress telemetry, not from the note.

## 8. Assessment Notes & Gaps

| Item | Status |
|---|---|
| Who builds `/etc/f-index` | Unknown. Not created by this binary. Either a separate staging tool or repurposed Synology indexer output. Recovering that tool would materially improve early detection. |
| The `_F` and `c2w`/`ctw` suffix variants | Unresolved. The note promises three suffixes; this build emits one. Self-exclusion entries from sibling builds follow a `<base>` / `<base>_F` / `c2w|ctw` pattern, implying companion binaries not present in this sample set. |
| Earlier file format (v1) | Recovered from dead code. `zw_write_footer_v1_dead @ 0x83E0` and `zw_rename_append_suffix_v1_dead @ 0xB740` are compiled in but unreferenced. They describe an earlier build that appended a bare 256-byte RSA blob (no magic, no length) and appended the suffix to the original filename instead of replacing it. Files from that build are invisible to the footer-magic rule. |
| Exfiltration capability | Absent from this binary. Claims in the note are unverified by code. |
| Initial access vector | Out of scope for a payload-only analysis. |
| Group attribution | Not attempted. Conclusions here derive from the binary alone; the LockBit exclusion list indicates borrowed builder configuration, not a LockBit affiliation. |
| Build date | Inferred only. The hardcoded clock fallback `1784990000 = 2026-07-25T14:33:20Z` sits inside the accepted execution window and is the closest available proxy. |

**Tracking recommendations.** Pivot on the RSA SPKI hash `66e37055247446e1f23efe62cf011b8cf77aa8aa0a937469319a5d8ce9053004` to link samples that share a key. A shared key across victims would indicate a single operator rather than an affiliate programme. Pivot on the 16-byte tweak constant `DF B3 07 AC 09 27 21 54 B1 E1 3B 58 7F 52 13 DE`. If it is stable across builds it is the best cross-build anchor available; if it varies, it becomes a per-build fingerprint. Watch the DLS onion for victim postings to correlate with the hardcoded victim ID model.

## 9. Indicator Appendix

# LockBit 5.0 (x64 hardened — "Corteva/Solstice" lure) — Technical Analysis Report

## 1. Key Judgements

This analysis identifies a **LockBit 5.0-generation x64 hardened build** featuring full obfuscation protections distinct from older 3.0-base variants. The sample masquerades as "Corteva / Solstice Google Photos" with administrator elevation request—a social-engineering distribution tactic.

The decrypted payload reveals a modern cryptographic stack: **X25519 key wrapping combined with ChaCha20-20 file encryption and Keccak-f1600/SHAKE256 key derivation**. This represents a significant departure from Sample 1's older SSSE3-ChaCha(22)+RSA-1024 approach.

The payload demonstrates extensive operational capabilities including multi-threaded chunked file encryption, RunPE process-hollowing targeting defrag.exe/svchost, ETW bypass, network self-propagation through ARP enumeration and port-scanning, event-log clearing, and service/process termination. A critical operator-origin signal emerges: the malware aborts execution on Russian-locale systems (UILang `0x419`) and specific GeoID values, consistent with CIS-exclusion patterns typical of LockBit RaaS affiliates.

Embedded configuration was successfully decrypted, revealing target drive scope, exclusion lists, VM-disk targeting (vhdx/avhdx), complete CLI argument sets, and operation-mode keywords. The ransom note and three onion addresses are MBA-encoded and assembled at runtime rather than embedded statically.

## 2. Actor / Tooling Assessment

The operator deploys the **modern LockBit 5.0 toolchain** with per-build customization:

- **Tailored masquerade:** Each build receives campaign-specific lure metadata while reusing the protected 5.0 core
- **Anti-analysis defenses:** The combination of MBA obfuscation, global-PRNG opaque predicates, import-by-hash, and per-string runtime crypto renders automated unpackers and sandbox analysis nearly ineffective
- **Elevation expectations:** The `requireAdministrator` manifest indicates the operator expects either user-initiated launch or exploitation of a delivery chain with elevation privileges

Existing LockBit 3.0 detection content—built around config-blob YARA signatures and residual templates—will not trigger on this 5.0-generation build.

## 3. Capability Summary

# Umbra Ransomware — CTI Report

## Executive Summary

Umbra is a Rust-based ransomware targeting Windows x86-64 systems. The malware encrypts files using ChaCha20-Poly1305 with RSA-2048 key wrapping, applies a `.umbra` extension, and displays a ransom screen.

Two critical characteristics:

1. **No independent network capability** — The payload contains no networking libraries, APIs, or functions. While it supports command execution via configuration, this build includes no commands configured.
2. **Incomplete operational setup** — The ransom note references a "contact portal" but provides no onion address, email, cryptocurrency wallet, or contact method. Three of ten configuration string slots remain empty.

## Key Findings

**Encryption Specifications:**
- Per-file ChaCha20-Poly1305 encryption with RSA-2048 wrapping
- 296-byte footer ending with magic bytes `RBMU`
- Files exceeding 256 MiB are skipped
- Modified ChaCha state constant (non-standard): prevents interoperability with stock implementations

**Disabled Capabilities:**
The binary contains compiled commands for shadow copy destruction, Defender neutralization, event log clearing, and service termination — but all corresponding flags are disabled in this build.

**Canary File Protection:**
Directories containing files named with these substrings are completely skipped: `canary`, `_decoy`, `honeytoken`, `eicar`, `testfile`, `honey`.

## Detection Indicators

**Most Valuable Signatures:**
- ChaCha state constant: `D5 46 E9 20 F6 39 B1 65 D2 4B FE 12 22 70 78 D9`
- Encrypted file footer: last 4 bytes `52 42 4D 55` with specific structural properties
- Configuration footer pattern with terminating magic bytes `21 44 4E 45`

**Sample Hash:**
- SHA-256: `976ea6c54c8eea1b7c3d1d5227c50fd16f301518fd659a9ee4a770568850f553`

## Incident Response Priorities

1. Check shadow copies and backups before assuming total loss
2. Inventory files exceeding 256 MiB (these remain intact)
3. Verify which directories contain canary files
4. Preserve encrypted files with originals for analysis
5. Scope impact using file size metadata without decryption

## Assessment

Evidence suggests this specific build was not deployed operationally — it contains test paths, mode banners, and empty configuration fields. However, the underlying engine represents production-grade malware.

## 1. Executive Summary

# EVEREST Ransomware — CTI Report

## Executive Summary

This analysis examines a protected Windows .NET 4.0 sample (SHA-256: `1df92bf4c967297d8a39fc3f619a56702ee96d5cf9196b8e1d5b3654746c6514`) self-identified as EVEREST ransomware through embedded strings including the `.everest` file extension, `EVERESTRANSOMWARE.txt` note filename, and contact email `everestaf@onionmail.org`.

## Key Findings

**Cryptographic Implementation:** the malware declares stronger primitives than actually deployed. Code specifies RSA-4096 and AES-256, but runtime execution uses RSA-1024 and AES-128 instead. The AES key and IV are derived via PBKDF2-HMACSHA1 using a 32-byte seed generated by `System.Random`, wrapped with RSA-1024 PKCS#1 v1.5.

**Pre-Encryption Operations:** before file encryption begins, the sample executes approximately 30 seconds of defensive disabling: Controlled Folder Access (CFA) disable, SMB1 protocol enablement, firewall rule modifications for file sharing and network discovery, registry changes enabling longer file paths and credential-token policies, and ICACLS commands granting Everyone full control over C:, D:, and Z: drives.

**Network Reconnaissance:** the malware discovers targets through five enumeration sources: `net view`, `NetDfsEnum`, `WNetEnumResource`, and WMI queries for shares and mapped drives. It parses the local ARP cache and broadcasts Wake-On-LAN UDP magic packets on ports 7 and 9 to discovered hosts before attempting SMB share connections.

**Process Protection:** the running process modifies its own security descriptor to insert a deny-all ACE for the World SID, rendering standard user-mode termination commands ineffective without DACL repair.

**Anti-Recovery Measures:** the sample invokes `vssadmin Delete Shadows` (or equivalent PowerShell commands) to eliminate volume shadow copies, iterates through system restore points for deletion, and removes backup files matching patterns like `*.VHD`, `*.bak`, and `*.bkf` across multiple drives.

## Pre-Encryption Detection Window

The combination of CFA disable, SMB1 enablement, firewall rule changes, and network-discovery service startup provides a 30–60 second action window before encryption begins. These commands are observable through PowerShell event logs (Event ID 4104) and process telemetry (Sysmon Event 1).

## Operational Artifacts

**Family-stable indicators** that persist across different Everest builds:
- Onion blog URL: `ransomocmou6mnbquqz44ewosbkjk3o5qjsl3orawojexfook2j7esad.onion`
- Contact email pattern: `everestaf@onionmail.org`
- File extension: `.everest`
- Note filename: `EVERESTRANSOMWARE.txt`
- Static PBKDF2 salt: `01 02 03 04 05 06 07 08`
- Worker thread loop intervals: 4 s, 15 s, 2.5 s

**Sample-specific pivots** (unique to this build): the RSA-1024 public key modulus and a hard-coded victim salutation embedded in the encrypted UserStrings heap.

## Notable Limitations

The note text claims approximately 1 TB of data exfiltration. However, the binary contains no socket imports, HTTP POST functionality, WinHTTP, or Ws2_32 calls — indicating the exfiltration claim exists only in text form without corresponding code implementation.

Similarly, while the `System.Random` seed-generation method and static PBKDF2 salt represent theoretical weaknesses, no practical exploitation pipeline is demonstrated that would recover plaintext without the operator's RSA private key.

## Detection Priorities

**Immediate (P0):** Isolate hosts executing the 3-of-5 pre-encryption commands (CFA disable, SMB1 enable, firewall modifications, mountvol usage, ICACLS grants). Snapshot memory to capture the AES Key and IV from the static fields `Program.AesKey` and `Program.AesIv` before self-delete completes. Block outbound UDP/7 and UDP/9 broadcast traffic.

**Short-term (P1):** Scan domain systems for `EVERESTRANSOMWARE.txt` in `C:\ProgramData`. Audit registry values `LongPathsEnabled`, `LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy`, and `EnableLinkedConnections`. Verify SMB1 status across all servers.

**Follow-up (P2):** Hunt for the literal string `[WALLNAME].bmp` in `%TEMP%`. Reconstruct lateral movement by reading `C:\ProgramData\<32-hex>` files, which contain the UNC paths added to the encryption queue.

## MITRE ATT&CK Mapping

The sample demonstrates techniques across multiple tactics: Command and Scripting Interpreter (PowerShell, CMD), Native API calls, Registry modification, Defense Evasion (Disable/Modify Tools, Hide Artifacts), System/Network Discovery, Lateral Movement via SMB, and Data Encryption for Impact, among others.

---

*This analysis covers a single protected sample and does not imply identical implementation across all Everest deployments. Family-level claims are restricted to indicators explicitly flagged as Family-scope.*

# BAVACAI Ransomware — CTI Report

## Executive Summary

BAVACAI is a Windows x64 ransomware employing RSA-2048 and ChaCha20 encryption with "moderate" operational sophistication but "amateur" engineering quality. The malware targets MSSQL/Hyper-V environments and contains multiple implementation flaws including typos in recovery-inhibition commands and verbose debug logging.

**Key findings:**
- Configuration uses plaintext ChaCha20 keys visible to string scanning
- Three shell commands fail silently due to typos (`SYSTEMSTABACKUP`, `recoverynabled`)
- Two taskkill entries are malformed, allowing PostgreSQL and SQLWriter to survive
- Exfiltration claims in ransom notes lack supporting code
- No lateral movement or persistence mechanisms present

## Notable Technical Flaws

**Configuration Security:** the 3119-byte JSON settings are encrypted with `TRUMPTRUMPTRUMPTRUMPTRUMPTRUMPTRUMP`[:32] as key and `PUTLERPUTLER`[:8] as nonce — both plaintext strings recoverable via string analysis without execution.

**Recovery Command Typos:**

- `taskkill -f -impostgres.exe` (malformed syntax)

Three-tier key hierarchy executes correctly but lacks message authentication codes. Per-file footers (1544 bytes) contain self-contained recovery material, making operator-side decryption trivial but victim-side recovery impossible without the master private key.

## Exfiltration Analysis

The ransom note claims "72-hour publication" of exfiltrated data, but no socket/HTTP-POST/WinHTTP imports exist. The only outbound call is a single GET to `api.ipify.org` for IP detection.

- File extension: `.BAVACAI`
- Ransom note: `WHATS_HAPPEND.txt` (typo preserved)
- Registry: `HKLM\SOFTWARE\PAIDMEMES` (PUBLIC/PRIVATE values)

Single-host destructive malware with no propagation, no exfiltration, and no lateral movement. The PDB path reveals developer infrastructure, and in-joke registry names suggest a solo developer rather than organized crime.

**Recommendations:** prioritize offline backup recovery; payment offers no operational advantage given single-point infrastructure and absent reputation mechanisms.

# VECT 2.0 Ransomware — CTI Report

## Executive Summary

VECT 2.0 is a Windows x64 ransomware employing ChaCha20 encryption with notable operational sophistication undermined by critical cryptographic flaws. The malware demonstrates "high" operational tradecraft through Active Directory exploitation but "low" cryptographic competence due to implementation errors.

## Critical Vulnerabilities

**Hardcoded Encryption Key:** the 256-bit ChaCha20 key is statically embedded in the binary's text section without runtime modification. This enables trivial decryption of files smaller than 128 KiB without operator cooperation.

**Lost-Nonce Flaw:** files exceeding 128 KiB are encrypted using four independent random nonces at quarter-intervals, but only the final nonce is retained. The first three nonces are discarded, making 75% of large encrypted files cryptographically unrecoverable regardless of ransom payment.

**Absent Exfiltration Code:** despite ransom-note threats of data leakage, the binary contains no socket, HTTP, DNS, or SMTP communication functions — only SMB share mounting for local file access.

## Operational Capabilities

The killchain spans ten PowerShell-based lateral-movement primitives covering WMI, DCOM, WinRM, scheduled tasks, and service installation. Additional defensive measures include Safe Mode persistence, Defender disablement, shadow copy deletion, and selective termination of backup and database services (CommVault, Veeam, MSSQL, Oracle, MySQL).

## Key IOCs

- **File Extension:** `.vect` suffix appended to encrypted files
- **Ransom Note:** `!!!READ_ME!!!.txt` in encrypted directories
- **Wallpaper Artifact:** `dvm3_wall.bmp` (1920×1080) in `%TEMP%`
- **Onion Domain:** `vectordntlcrlmfkcm4alni734tbcrnd5lk44v6sp4lqal6noqrgnbyd.onion`

## Verdict

VECT 2.0 constitutes a destructive incident rather than a recoverable encryption scenario. Files larger than 128 KiB cannot be recovered through payment due to architectural encryption flaws, rendering the threat primarily a data-destruction vector despite sophisticated lateral movement capabilities.

# IronChain 3.0 Ransomware — CTI Brief

## Executive Summary

| | |
|---|---|
| **Family** | IronChain 3.0 |
| **Platform** | Windows x64 (PE32+, Python 3.14 PyInstaller) |
| **Encryption** | AES-GCM intermittent + RSA-4096-OAEP runtime-generated |
| **Sophistication (Operational)** | Technically advanced but poorly engineered — comprehensive persistence (6 layers), SafeBoot survival, SMB/WMI lateral movement, MFT destruction, UEFI+BIOS boot destruction, but critical bugs and auto-sabotage |
| **Sophistication (Cryptographic)** | Fundamentally broken — multi-layer cipher shifts discarded, runtime RSA key never exfiltrated |
| **Exfiltration** | None observed — no C2 communication, networking limited to lateral movement and DDoS |
| **Recovery feasibility** | Zero — even with operator cooperation, shift values lost make files unrecoverable |
| **Sample SHA-256** | `2d57b05e8fbcae3da196ed972074577fa6604ba7f3afcadbf79b94c8f8f6de22` |

## Critical Weaknesses

### 1. Multi-layer cipher with lost shift values

The encryption pipeline applies a pseudo-cipher layer before AES-GCM that destroys recoverability:

```python
def mc(data):
    layers = random.randint(2, 7)        # 2-7 random passes
    shifts = []
    result = bytearray(data)
    for _ in range(layers):
        shift = random.randint(-255, 255)
        shifts.append(shift)
        for i in range(len(result)):
            if random.random() < 0.75:   # 75% of bytes shifted per layer
                result[i] = (result[i] + shift) & 0xFF
    return bytes(result), shifts
```

The calling function `ef()` discards the second return value (`shifts`) with `_`. These shifts are never written to disk, never transmitted, and `random` is not seeded. The transformation is **mathematically irreversible**. Even if the operator possessed the RSA private key and cooperated fully, victim files remain permanently unrecoverable.

### 2. Runtime RSA key generation with no exfiltration

The ransomware generates a fresh 4096-bit RSA keypair at startup via `RSA.generate(4096)`. The private key exists only in process memory and is never serialized, transmitted, or stored. No C2 channels exist. The private key is lost when the process terminates — no entity can decrypt victim files, including the operator.

### 3. MFT destruction parallel to encryption

Function `em()` overwrites 1 GB of the NTFS Master File Table with AES-CTR using a random key that is never saved:

```
mft_start_sector = 786432 × 8  # typical NTFS MFT location
mft_size_sectors = 1073741824 // 512  # 1 GB
```

Runs as a parallel daemon thread during encryption, destroying filesystem metadata for all files, including those not yet encrypted. Recovery tools cannot reconstruct file names or directory structures.

### 4. Boot destruction before encryption completes

Overwrites both BIOS and UEFI boot loaders immediately after setup:
- **BIOS MBR:** 512-byte custom boot sector with "CHAINED - PAY TO DECRYPT" message (off-by-one bug prevents display)
- **UEFI:** zeroes first 512 bytes of `bootmgfw.efi` on all EFI System Partitions

Combined with `bcdedit /set {default} safeboot minimal`, the machine becomes permanently unbootable regardless of encryption completion.

## Sample Fingerprint

| | |
|---|---|
| SHA-256 | `2d57b05e8fbcae3da196ed972074577fa6604ba7f3afcadbf79b94c8f8f6de22` |
| MD5 | `71318a233ae849db62eb4037486ba3ff` |
| Size | 11,282,718 bytes (11 MB) |
| Format | PE32+ x64 PyInstaller bundle |
| Python version | 3.14.4 (magic `2b0e0d0a`) |
| Mutex | `IronChainMutex_<8_random_chars>` |

## Killchain at a Glance

```
[1] Admin check      OpenProcessToken + GetTokenInformation(TokenElevation)
[2] Self-relocate    C:\Windows\System32\<random_subfolder>\<MS_binary_name>.exe
[3] Process critical NtSetInformationProcess BreakOnTermination (kill = BSOD)
[4] Defense disable  Kill 39 processes, stop 16 services, IFEO cmd.exe -> svchost.exe
[5] Persistence      6 layers: Run keys, Winlogon shell, service, SafeBoot survival
[6] Boot destruction BIOS MBR + UEFI bootmgfw.efi overwrite
[7] Recovery disable vssadmin delete, bcdedit safeboot minimal, registry tamper
[8] Network isolate  50 sites to hosts file (incl. torproject.org auto-sabotage)
[9] UI display       HTA multilingual ransom note + wallpaper + text note
[10] Keyboard lock   WH_KEYBOARD_LL hook swallows all WM_KEYDOWN
[11] Encrypt         Intermittent AES-GCM (>1.1MB: first 500KB + random 50KB + last 500KB)
[12] MFT wipe        Parallel AES-CTR destruction of filesystem metadata
[13] Lateral move    SMB + WMI propagation to discovered subnets (50 thread pool)
[14] DDoS flood      320 threads target local gateway + external host
[15] Force shutdown  Kill explorer, 4-minute timer, shutdown /s /f
```

## Detection & Response — Priority IOCs

| Type | Value |
|---|---|
| File extension | `.Chained` (appended to original) |
| File header | `CHAINED_6617-382+819=...!_(13RANDOM)` (38 bytes) |
| Ransom note | `PLEASEREADTHIS.txt` (Desktop + C:\Users\Public) |
| HTA interface | `IronChain.hta` (C:\Users\Public) |
| Wallpaper | `%TEMP%\IronChain_wallpaper.bmp` (PNG content, 1920×1080) |
| Infection marker | `C:\ProgramData\IRONCHAIN\time.dat` |
| Service name | `IronChainSecurity` |
| Mutex | `IronChainMutex_<8_chars>` |

**High-signal behaviors:** `bcdedit /set {default} safeboot minimal` from a non-admin tool; registry write to `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SafeBoot\{Minimal,Network}\IronChainSecurity`; `NtSetInformationProcess` with `ProcessBreakOnTermination`; IFEO `cmd.exe` -> `Debugger=svchost.exe`; raw disk access to `\\.\PhysicalDrive0`; raw volume writes to `\\.\C:` (MFT region); `WH_KEYBOARD_LL` hook; mass SMB share access to `\\<subnet>\C$\Users\Public\`; PowerShell WMI remote process creation; hosts-file modification blocking security vendors.

**Response priorities:**

2. **Immediate isolation** — block SMB from infected hosts; the 50-thread scanner spreads fast.

# Aurora Ransomware — Technical Analysis

## Executive Summary

Aurora is a multi-platform ransomware family (Windows/Linux/ESXi) compiled as a Windows x64 binary using Mingw-w64. This ~154 KB executable demonstrates sophisticated encryption mechanisms coupled with aggressive privilege escalation and file targeting strategies, while maintaining minimal stealth characteristics.

## Sample Identification

**SHA-256:** `81ca5fc6b55accdbc44266d66bd72c7c4152a75b215593adc433d51250054333`

PE32+ x86-64 GUI application built with reproducible-build techniques. Contains no PDB path and implements no anti-debugging, anti-virtualization, or string obfuscation — static analysis is straightforward.

## Cryptographic Architecture

Hybrid encryption model:
- **Asymmetric layer:** RSA-4096 with OAEP-SHA512 padding wraps per-file key material
- **Symmetric layer:** ChaCha20 stream cipher with SSE2 optimization handles bulk encryption
- **Key derivation:** per-file random material (40 bytes total) generated via thread-local CTR_DRBG

Each file receives a fresh 32-byte ChaCha20 key and 8-byte nonce, eliminating nonce-reuse vulnerabilities across encrypted files.

## Privilege Escalation Mechanisms

Three-tier privilege-elevation strategy:
1. **Primary:** enables `SeBackupPrivilege` and `SeRestorePrivilege` at startup to bypass NTFS ACLs
2. **Secondary:** activates `SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege` when access is initially denied
3. **ACL rewriting:** modifies file ownership to `BUILTIN\Administrators` and grants full DACL permissions

This leaves permanent ownership changes even after potential file recovery.

## File Encryption Process

- **Intelligent targeting:** encrypts all extensions except `exe`, `dll`, and `iso`
- **Intermittent encryption:** variable percentages by file size (3–100%), positions distributed via sqrt-based recurrence
- **Resume capability:** persists per-chunk completion bitmap at offset `file_size + 534`, enabling safe interruption and resumption
- **Directory exclusions:** skips system folders (Windows, Boot, System Volume Information, $Recycle.Bin, etc.)

## Recovery Inhibition Tactics

Disables system recovery through shell-executed commands: shadow copy deletion via `vssadmin` and `wmic`, shadow storage constraint via size limiting (401 MB max), and System Restore task disablement via `schtasks`. All recovery destruction occurs via `cmd.exe /C` rather than in-process COM/WMI.

## Network Infrastructure

**Onion address:** `ijexszhscln27nl263lmcd7tx3jttkhm4wjhd4e3y6r4csdbfyeprvid.onion`

The ransom note claims data exfiltration, yet the binary contains no HTTP, socket, or network APIs — exfiltration, if performed, occurs through separate tooling prior to ransomware deployment.

## Operational Characteristics

- Multi-instance capable (no named mutexes prevent concurrent execution)
- Multi-threaded design (default worker count = `max(4, 2×CPU cores)`)
- SMB enumeration: discovers and encrypts accessible network shares via `WNetEnumResourceW`
- No process termination (lacks service-stopping/process-killing)
- No persistence (does not self-delete or establish reboot-time execution)

## Ransom Note

`!!!README!!!DO_NOT_DELETE.txt` — deposited at drive roots and within every successfully scanned directory. Provides the onion URL and a 32-hex access key.

## Indicators of Compromise

- Footer magic at `EOF - 542 - N + 1`: `4A 94 37 43` (LE format)
- Footer version byte: `03`
- Bitmap location: `file_size + 534`
- Distinctive strings: usage banner with Linux-style invocation, `Mode: ENCRYPT (compiled-in)`, CTR_DRBG personalization `thread_drbg_%d`, recovery commands targeting `vssadmin`, `wmic`, `schtasks`

## MITRE ATT&CK

T1486 (data encryption), T1490 (recovery inhibition), T1134.002 (token manipulation), T1222.001 (permission modification), T1135 (network share discovery), T1083 (file discovery), T1059.003 (command shell execution).

## Assessment

Aurora demonstrates competent encryption engineering with correct cryptographic implementations and sophisticated access-control bypassing. The cross-platform codebase signals infrastructure-targeting capability. The absence of stealth mechanisms suggests operators prioritize speed and efficiency over evasion, relying on rapid deployment and broad file targeting for impact maximization.

#### 5.1 Key exchange (`main.load_config` @ `0x517740`)

| Parameter                    | Value                                                                                                                                                                      |
| ---------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Algorithm**                | X25519 (ECDH over Curve25519)                                                                                                                                              |
| **Implementation**           | `crypto/ecdh` stdlib — `x25519Curve.GenerateKey`, `PrivateKey.PublicKey`, `x25519Curve.NewPublicKey`, `PrivateKey.ECDH`                                                    |
| **Attacker public key (K1)** | `cdbe4aed37c98d67a005ef469e7e0586e0ff8973b91a8d577d320e67cf46b572` (32 B, `.rdata` → config gob)                                                                           |
| **Ephemeral private key**    | generated each run via `crypto/rand.Reader` (not exported, lives in RAM)                                                                                                   |
| **Ephemeral public key**     | derived via `PublicKey()` — **written into every file's footer** (32 B at +56, cf §5.4) so the attacker can recompute `shared_secret = ECDH(attacker_priv, ephemeral_pub)` |
| **Output shared secret**     | `shared_secret = ECDH(ephemeral_priv, attacker_pub)` — **32 B** used as the **KEK** (Key-Encryption-Key)                                                                   |

`load_config` step-by-step:

1. Builds a `bytes.Buffer` initialized with `1F 8B 08 00 00` (5 bytes); `Write(5×0x00)` → full gzip header (10 bytes, all zeros after magic).
2. `qmemcpy` copies 4,096 B `aT_0` blob (`0x55ECBF`) into local buffer; `Write(v77)` appends it → `bytes.Buffer` holds 4,106 bytes (`1F 8B 08 00 00 00 00 00 00 00` + 4,096 B blob).
3. `compress/gzip.NewReader` decompresses into 1,522 bytes of gob plaintext.
4. `encoding/gob.NewDecoder(gz).Decode(&EC)` where `EC struct { K1 [32]uint8; EX string; NN string; NT []byte }`.
5. `crypto/ecdh.X25519().GenerateKey(crypto/rand.Reader)` → `ephemeral_priv`.
6. `ephemeral_priv.PublicKey()` → `ephemeral_pub` (32 B). Stored in global `g_ephemeral_x25519_pubkey` @ `0x6C80C0` (used at §5.4 to write into each file's footer).
7. `X25519().NewPublicKey(K1[:])` → `attacker_pub_obj` (parses bytes → curve point).
8. `ephemeral_priv.ECDH(attacker_pub_obj)` → `shared_secret` (32 B). Stored in global `g_shared_secret` @ `0x6C80E0`, used by `encode_file` as KEK.

- `"Config unpack error."` (gzip failure) — wrapped into an `errors.errorString`
- `"Config decode error."` (gob failure) — idem
- ECDH errors are propagated

##### 5.4.1 Where the ephemeral_pub lives — data-flow validated

Traced across `main.load_config` and `main.encode_file`:

  crypto_cipher_newGCMWithNonceAndTagSize(block, 12, 16)

1. Read the 1,024 B footer.
2. `ephemeral_pub = footer[+56 : +56+32]`
3. `shared_secret = ECDH(attacker_priv, ephemeral_pub)` (via X25519)
4. `file_key = AES-GCM.Open(key=shared_secret, nonce=footer[+8 : +8+12], ct=footer[+88 : +88+48])` → recovers the 32 B per-file key
5. `plaintext = AES-CTR(key=file_key, IV=footer[+8 : +8+16])` over `file[0 : filesize-1024]`

##### 5.4.2 Caveat for PARTIAL files

If magic = `0x3828AC45` (partial in progress), footer contains `file_key` **in cleartext** at offset +24 (not yet sealed). An analyst who snapshots file at this stage can decrypt it **without `attacker_priv`**. Seal only happens on final pass.

#### 5.5 Intermittent encryption (`encode_file` loop)

- **Chunk size**: `chunk_size = (perc << 8 / 100) << 12` bytes. Concrete mapping (4 KB-aligned except rounding):
- `perc = 1` → 8,192 B (8 KB)
- `perc = 25` → 256 KB
- `perc = 50` → 512 KB
- `perc = 100` → 1 MiB (`-fast` forces this)
- **Stride**: chunks written at offsets `chunk_counter × 1 MiB` — fixed 1 MiB stride regardless of `chunk_size`. So at `perc = 1`, each 1 MiB block has only ~7 KB encrypted at start, rest untouched. At `perc = 100`, encryption contiguous.
- **Loop**:
 1. `time.Now()` (t0) — throttling start
 2. `os.File.ReadAt(buf, chunk_size, offset_read)`; skip if `< 1024 B` remain (to not overwrite footer)
 3. `os.File.Seek(offset_write, 0)` (same position as read, minus 1,024 B footer padding)
 4. CTR encrypt `buf[:n-1024]`
 5. `os.File.Write(buf[:n-1024])`
 6. `os.File.Seek(offset_read, 0)` (reposition for next iteration)
 7. `chunk_counter++`; `os.File.Write(chunk_counter)` (4 B at file end)
 8. Update global counters (bytes_encrypted, in 1 MiB or tail slices)
 9. `dt = Now() - t0`; if `dt < 10 ms` → `time.Sleep(1 ms × min(999, ...))` (**auto I/O throttling**, avoids disk flood triggering behavioural detection)
- **Exit conditions**:
- `byte_6C7CA3[0]` (`-fast` flag) → stop after 1 pass (flag short-circuits CTR loop past first chunk)
- `chunk_counter == 51200` — guardrail (max 200 GB at 4 MB chunks, but practically caps protection against monster files)
- `ctx.Done()` — signal propagated (Ctrl+C or wrapper equivalent)
- **Finalisation** (on loop exit):
 1. `Seek(-1024, SEEK_END)` → positions at footer
 2. `*magic = 0x741FBE88` (complete)
 3. `memcpy(footer[+56..+88], g_ephemeral_x25519_pubkey[:32])`
 4. `AES-256-GCM.Seal(nonce=footer[+8 : +8+12], plaintext=per_file_key, aad=nil)` → 48 B (ct 32 + tag 16)
 5. Copy sealed output to `footer[+88..+136]`
 6. `AES-256-CTR.XORKeyStream(footer[+136 : +136+884])` — encrypts original filename in place
 7. `binary.Write(file, footer)` — final 1,024 B dump

#### 5.6 Skip rules

- File `< 1024 B` → skipped with error `"stat '%s' err: so small, %d"`
- File already marked `0x741FBE88` (complete) → skipped (returns size)
- File marked `0x3828AC45` (partial in progress) → **resumed** (reads key/IV/chunk_counter from footer, continues CTR loop)

### 15. Summary

**m3rx (variant `LOCAL`)** is a **Go-compiled Windows x64 ransomware**, minimalist on evasion side but well-structured on crypto and anti-forensics. The whole flow — CLI parsing, config, crypto, file enumeration, threading pipeline, self-delete — fits in **30 `main.*` functions** (~30 KB user code) built on Go stdlib (`crypto/aes`, `crypto/cipher`, `crypto/ecdh`, `encoding/gob`, `compress/gzip`, `os/exec`, `sync`, `context`). No packer, no code obfuscation, Go symbols preserved via pclntab ⇒ fast analysis after Lumina.

**Sound, classic cryptographic architecture**, two layers:

1. **Inter-file**: X25519 ECDH with embedded attacker pubkey (gzip+gob 4,096 B blob at `0x55ECBF`); one ephemeral pair per instance (= per victim) ⇒ `shared_secret` 32 B stable for whole session, used as KEK.
2. **Intra-file**: per-file key 32 B + IV 16 B random, AES-256-CTR in chunks (`(perc<<8)/100<<12` B, throttled ≤999 ms), finalised by AES-256-GCM wrap of file-key (nonce = first 12 B of IV field, i.e. `footer[+8 .. +20]`) + AES-CTR of original filename; magics `0x3828AC45` (partial) / `0x741FBE88` (complete) at start of 1,024 B footer.

Operational strategy **"gentle but thorough"**: **partial encryption by default** (1%), `-fast` to bypass (100%); auto throttling for I/O stealth; rename to `<16 random chars>.8hmlsewu` + Tor victim-ID to avoid trivial inter-file correlation. Removable/fixed/remote drives enumerated (skip CD/RAM). **No** service stop, **no** kill-listed processes; only reaction to locked files is **Restart Manager** at tail (`RmShutdown(FORCE)`).

**Prominent anti-forensics**: VSS deletion via **embedded WMI shellcode** (gzip → JIT via `VirtualProtect`+`CreateThread`), silent recycle bin empty, **PowerShell self-delete** with 10 MiB random overwrite loop before `Remove-Item`. **No** online C2 (victim ↔ operator via Tor Browser out-of-band); **no** exfiltration (the "files stolen" wording relies on external stealer not in binary).

Simple guardrail **T1480**: refuses to run in Medium IL — requires prior elevation (UAC already consented); global mutex `CRC32("kek"+Hostname())` prevents multi-instance. **RECOVERY_NOTES.TXT** dropped ONLY in `Desktop`/`Documents` (case-insensitive), contains onion + unique chat path (`WAJCTZ6FOJF75KB5XVRYBFERX6`) + Tox, with double-extortion rhetoric (publication + sharing with competitors).

**Sophistication level**: medium. Solid crypto and anti-forensics, but:
- No anti-debug, no anti-VM, no anti-sandbox.
- No propagation (SMB, WMI/PsExec, WMIExec).
- No AV/service kill.
- Strings in clear except config and shellcode.
- Characteristic misspelling "**complited**" in final log.

**Operational risk level**: high as soon as attacker lands HIGH IL run — binary does exactly what's needed to make recovery impossible without attacker's X25519 private key, and wipes traces. Incident-response window is **short** (fire-and-forget self-delete at end of run).

# Panzer — Reglas del programa de afiliados (OSINT)

*Reglamento del programa RaaS tal y como lo publica el propio grupo, recogido por RansomLook. Material de inteligencia (política del programa), no operativo.*

## Producto (panel de afiliado)
- Panel de control individual por afiliado con enlace propio.
- Dashboard con monitorizacion automatica (ingresos totales, saldo disponible, builds activos, tickets abiertos, miembros del equipo y actividad reciente).
- Pestana Wallet: deposito/retirada, historial de transacciones y saldo.
- Pestana Builds: soporta **Windows, Linux, ESXi y FreeBSD**; subida local de builds; chat autogenerado por build con generador de enlace onion; chat protegido por ID/password; adjuntos; generacion de factura de pago BTC dentro del chat del build (el pago se acredita al wallet del afiliado y la factura se envia al chat de negociacion para aprobacion); historial de accesos que registra si algun miembro de la empresa victima entra al chat.
- Pestana Blog: creacion de posts (con aprobacion del equipo), muestras, temporizador de cuenta atras, enlace de descarga, nombre y tamano de datos, logo y descripcion; posts destacados/fijados.
- Pestanas Support, News, Team (cuentas para miembros) y Rules.

## Reparto
- **80% para el afiliado, 20% para Panzer.** Deducido automaticamente de cada pago.

## Reglas de entrada (senales CTI)
- Prohibido atacar paises de la **CIS**.
- Prohibido atacar empresas que involucren a menores de 18 anos.
- Prohibido violar cualquier regla del apartado de normas (baneo = enlace del panel deja de funcionar).
- Inactividad la primera semana = desactivacion automatica de la cuenta.

## Acceso
- Solicitud de entrada por Tox (contacto en su sitio).

> Fuente: RansomLook — RaaS Rules (Panzer). La exclusion de la CIS es una senal de atribucion habitual en programas RaaS de habla rusa.

# Vexy — Reglas del programa de afiliados (OSINT)

*Reglamento/oferta del programa RaaS tal y como lo publica el grupo, recogido por RansomLook. Material de inteligencia (descripcion del programa), no operativo.*

**Lenguaje del locker:** Rust

## Locker Windows (capacidades declaradas)
- Cifrado hibrido AES-256 (datos) + RSA (envoltura de clave).
- Cobertura de discos locales y recursos de red.
- Exclusiones: carpetas/archivos/extensiones "blancas".
- Terminacion selectiva de servicios y procesos.
- Borrado de espacio libre; auto-borrado tras ejecucion.
- Personalizacion (icono/fondo), notificacion via impresora, monitorizacion en tiempo real.

## Locker Linux
- Mismo cifrado hibrido; cifrado de recursos SMB/NFS y datos locales.
- Exclusiones, terminacion de servicios criticos, borrado de espacio libre, auto-borrado.

## Locker ESXi
- Cifrado dirigido a datastores de maquinas virtuales; terminacion de servicios VMware.
- Auto-borrado y borrado de logs de eventos.

## Panel de control
- Accesible por Tor (onion); herramienta de configuracion/compilacion de builds por plataforma.
- Analitica detallada, gestion de cuenta, comunicacion con clientes (negociaciones/tickets), soporte 24/7, multi-idioma.

## Acceso
- Mecanismo por **codigo de invitacion** (sitio privado).
- Coste unico de registro: **200 USD** en BTC; entrega instantanea y automatica del codigo.
